title: Case study: reading Apple's / Vinamilk's financial statements
subtitle: Applying the three statements to a real example
openingQuestion: Apple holds hundreds of billions of USD in cash but still borrows money. Why?
openingOptions: Because Apple is close to bankruptcy
Because its cash sits abroad, and borrowing domestically to buy back shares is tax-efficient
Because Apple doesn't actually have enough cash on hand to fund everything it wants to do next
explanation: Reading a real financial statement is very different from studying each ratio in isolation: numbers only mean something once placed next to each other and next to context. A classic example is Apple holding a mountain of cash while also borrowing to buy back shares - reading each line alone looks contradictory, but most of that cash sat abroad and bringing it home would be taxed, so borrowing domestically was cheaper. The general lesson is to always ask why before concluding good or bad.

diagram.label: Borrows domestically to fund buybacks instead of repatriating

realWorldExample.description: Apple: Revenue ~$400 billion, Gross Margin ~45%, OCF ~$110 billion, FCF ~$100 billion, buybacks ~$90 billion/year. This is the strongest free-cash-flow machine in the world.

quiz.question: Vinamilk has a Gross Margin of ~45%. What does that mean?
options: Every 100 dong of cost generates 45 dong of extra revenue that period
Every 100 dong of assets generates 45 dong of revenue each year
Every 100 dong of revenue leaves 45 dong of net profit
Every 100 dong of revenue leaves 45 dong after cost of goods sold
quiz.explanation: A 45% Gross Margin means good pricing power or low production cost. For Vietnam's dairy industry, this margin is quite high - reflecting Vinamilk's strong brand and operating efficiency.

quiz.question: The Apple/Vinamilk case shows two very different companies in industry and scale. What is the most important shared lesson for applying the three-statement analysis framework to ANY business?
options: The three statements provide one analytical framework applicable to any industry
Every single industry needs its own completely separate, purpose-built set of analytical metrics
Large and small companies simply cannot be compared with each other
Absolute figures matter more than ratios when comparing companies
quiz.explanation: This is the core value of learning to read financial statements: once you understand the logic connecting the Income Statement, Balance Sheet, and Cash Flow Statement, you can apply it to analyse ANY business - from a US tech giant to a Vietnamese dairy company - even though each industry's specific benchmarks will differ.

quiz.question: Why did Apple once borrow domestically to buy back shares despite sitting on a mountain of cash abroad?
options: Because US law bans companies from using cash to buy back treasury stock
Because bringing the money back to the US would trigger repatriation tax, while borrowing domestically was cheaper
Because Apple couldn't legally transfer any funds at all from its overseas subsidiary accounts back into the United States
Because buying back shares with borrowed money enjoyed a much larger tax break
quiz.explanation: Before the 2017 tax reform, repatriating foreign profit was taxed very heavily. Borrowing in the US at low interest rates was cheaper than that tax bill - a purely calculated capital-allocation decision, unrelated to any shortage of cash.

quiz.question: What does Vinamilk's roughly 45% Gross Margin tell you?
options: The company's net profit reaches about 45% of its annual revenue
The company's selling and administrative costs make up about 45% of revenue
It has pricing power or a lower production cost than industry peers
The company is selling below cost to grab market share in the industry
quiz.explanation: A high gross margin in the consumer-goods industry usually comes from a strong brand (customers accept a higher price) or large production scale (lower unit cost). It's a measure of competitive advantage before operating costs are even considered.

quiz.question: When FCF is close to OCF at a company, what does that reflect about its business model?
options: The company has very large depreciation, so cash flow is much higher than profit
The company is deliberately cutting all forms of investment and will soon lose its competitive edge to rivals
The company borrows heavily, so most of its cash flow goes to paying interest
Low CapEx - the company doesn't need much fixed-asset investment to generate revenue
quiz.explanation: Software, brands, platforms - models that generate cash without constantly having to build new plants - have FCF close to OCF. By contrast, airlines or steel companies always show a large gap because they must keep reinvesting heavily.

quiz.question: Two companies have equal revenue; one has a 45% gross margin, the other 15%. What's the most correct conclusion?
options: You need to check operating costs next; a high gross margin doesn't guarantee high profit
The company with the 45% gross margin is guaranteed to end up with higher final net profit than the other one
The company with the 15% gross margin is losing money and will soon exit the market
The two companies have equivalent business efficiency since revenue is the same
quiz.explanation: A high gross margin eaten up by selling costs still leaves a thin final profit - that's the story for many consumer brands that must spend heavily on advertising. The gap between gross margin and operating margin is where the real story is told.

keyTakeaways: Apple: strong OCF, FCF close to OCF, continuous buybacks
Vinamilk: high gross margin → pricing power or production efficiency
A case study helps put theory into practice

practicePrompt.question: Analysing Apple's real financial statements, you see very large OCF, CapEx relatively small compared with OCF (so FCF is close to OCF), and the company spending tens of billions of USD every year buying back shares. What does this show about Apple's business model?
options: Apple is struggling to find new investment opportunities, forcing it to use cash for buybacks instead
Apple generates far more cash than its CapEx needs, so it can keep handing the surplus to shareholders
Continuous buybacks are always a bad sign showing management doesn't know how to use cash effectively
Large OCF with FCF close to OCF is unusual and worrying for investors
practicePrompt.explanation: Apple: strong OCF, FCF close to OCF (CapEx low relative to cash generated), continuous buybacks - characteristic of a mature company with a capital-efficient business model that doesn't need heavy reinvestment to sustain growth, leaving it plenty of cash to return to shareholders.

summary.keyIdea: Apple: strong OCF, FCF close to OCF, continuous buybacks
summary.commonMistake: Reading a concept as a phrase to memorise rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: Vinamilk: high gross margin → pricing power or production efficiency

application.title: Try reading a real set of financial statements
application.message: Open the financial statements of a company whose products you use (for example Apple, Vinamilk, or any listed company), skim through all three statements in 10 minutes, and write down one thing that surprised you.
application.secondary: The first read will feel confusing - that's normal, just read it a few more times.

sections.text: Theory only really sinks in once applied to real numbers. This lesson walks through analysing the financial statements of two companies at opposite ends of the world: Apple - the American tech giant with a mountain of cash, and Vinamilk - Vietnam's leading dairy company with an impressive profit margin.
Step 1: read the P&L - what does the margin say?

Vinamilk has a Gross Margin around 40-45%: meaning for every 100 dong of revenue, after subtracting raw-milk cost and production cost, 40-45 dong remains as gross profit. This is high for the consumer-goods industry generally, reflecting a strong brand (pricing power - the ability to sell above production cost) and efficient large-scale plant operations. Apple has an even higher Gross Margin, around 45%, despite selling hardware - thanks to its closed ecosystem (App Store, services) and extremely strong brand pricing.
Step 2: read the Balance Sheet - asset and debt structure

Apple owns hundreds of billions of USD in cash and short-term investment securities, yet also carries significant borrowing - a curiosity for a beginner. The reason: most of Apple's cash was generated and held at its foreign subsidiaries; instead of bringing it back to the US and paying heavy repatriation tax, Apple borrowed domestically at low rates to fund share buybacks - a sophisticated tax-optimisation and capital-structure strategy.
Step 3: read the Cash Flow Statement - cash-flow quality

Both companies have very strong OCF relative to their scale. Apple's OCF runs around $110 billion/year, and because its CapEx is relatively small relative to its revenue scale (Apple doesn't manufacture its own hardware but outsources through Foxconn and other partners), Apple's FCF is close to its OCF - around $100 billion. This is one of the largest free-cash-flow machines in the world.
Step 4: read the capital-allocation strategy through Financing Cash Flow

Apple uses most of its FCF to buy back shares - around $90 billion/year - clearly visible in a very large negative Financing Cash Flow. This signals the company believes there's no better reinvestment opportunity than returning cash to shareholders through buybacks (which raise EPS by shrinking shares outstanding) and dividends. Vinamilk also has a tradition of paying high, steady cash dividends, reflecting a similar capital-allocation philosophy despite its much smaller scale.

items: High Gross Margin (Apple, Vinamilk) → strong brand, pricing power
Apple keeps cash abroad, borrows domestically to buy back shares tax-efficiently
Strong OCF, relatively low CapEx → FCF close to OCF (a characteristic of 'asset-light' companies)
Large negative Financing Cash Flow from buybacks/dividends = confidence about future cash flow

left.label: Apple
left.text: Revenue ~$400 billion, Gross Margin ~45%, OCF ~$110 billion, FCF ~$100 billion, buybacks ~$90 billion/year. An 'asset-light' model thanks to outsourced manufacturing, keeping invested capital low relative to the cash it generates.

right.label: Vinamilk
right.text: Gross Margin ~40-45%, running its own large-scale production plants, relatively higher CapEx than Apple, but still maintaining stable positive FCF to pay a regular annual dividend.

sections.label: The main lesson from this case study
sections.text: Reading financial statements isn't about finding one single 'pretty' number, but about understanding the story behind it: how the business makes money (P&L), what it owns and owes (Balance Sheet), and how it actually generates/uses cash (Cash Flow). These three pieces fit together to tell a complete story.

lines: Apple and Vinamilk differ in scale and industry, but both illustrate a shared principle: high Gross Margin, strong FCF, and disciplined capital allocation are signs of a quality business.
